newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: U.S. wheat crop not freeze-damaged as much as first thought.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wheat crop not freeze-damaged as much as first thought.

text.p: The 1997 U.S. wheat crop has not been as badly hit by freeze damage as the market has assumed and output should be 2.38 billion bushels versus 2.28 billion bushels in 1996, consultant Willard Sparks said Tuesday.
"Our assessment is that people are over-reacting and the wheat freeze damage is not as bad as people think," Sparks, head of Sparks Companies of Memphis, Tenn., told a conference in Argentina.
Sparks expects U.S. wheat carryout of 801 million bushels in 1997, up from 484 million bushels the previous year.
Total world wheat carryout should also rise, to 129.3 million tonnes in 1997/98, from 120.0 million tonnes in 1996/97.
World wheat production should slip slightly to 580.8 million tonnes in 1997/98, from 581.6 million tonnes the previous year.
Sparks said that drought damage in France was minimal.

"It's very hard for it to get too dry for wheat in France," he said, predicting a combined crop by the 15 European Union members of 98.7 million tonnes in 1997/98, down from 99.3 million tonnes in 1996/97.
Canadian wheat output should slip to 26.3 million tonnes in 1997/98, from 30.5 million tonnes, while Australia's crop should fall to 19.5 million tonnes from 23.5 million tonnes in 1996/97.
Sparks added he expected Argentine wheat production of 12.7 million tonnes in 1997/98, down from 15.6 million tonnes.
Wheat prices should be relatively stable, Sparks said.

"We don't see any real upward pressure on wheat. We don't really see any demand change," he said. He added, "We don't see anything really exciting about wheat, unless we get a demand kick or something."
